title: Kano Writes Judo
bigQuestion: How did one teacher in Tokyo turn many old fighting schools into a school subject with written ranks and rules?

story.title: Notes on a Temple Desk
story.kicker: In 1882 a young teacher in Tokyo sorts the notes of two old schools into one new plan.
paragraphs: It is 1882 in Tokyo, Japan. Kanō Jigorō is 21 years old. He has just finished his studies at Tokyo University. He rents rooms at Eishōji, a small Buddhist temple in the city.

Kanō has studied jujutsu for years. He trained in two old schools, Tenshin Shin'yō-ryū and Kitō-ryū. Each school kept its own lessons and its own secrets. Each teacher passed them to a few chosen students.
Kanō wants something different. He wants lessons that any student can learn in order. He wants a name, a plan and ranks that anyone can read. He calls his new school the Kodokan and his subject judo.
Only a few students come at first. The room is small and the mats are few. But Kanō keeps writing and teaching. Within a few years, schools and police across Japan know the Kodokan's name.
story.think: Why might a teacher want lessons written down in order instead of kept secret?

lessons.title: Many Old Schools
lessons.mainIdea: Before judo, Japan had many separate jujutsu schools, each called a ryū.
reading: In Japan from the 1600s to the 1800s, many teachers taught *jujutsu*. The word means the gentle art or the soft skill. It was a set of ways to handle an attacker without a weapon, or with a small one.

Each teaching family was called a *ryū*, which means a school or a stream. A ryū had its own name, founder and lessons. Records list many different jujutsu ryū in this long era, called the Edo period.
A ryū often gave written scrolls to its best students. These scrolls named the lessons and the teachers before them. The scrolls were private. Outsiders could not easily read them or join.

words.d: old Japanese arts of handling an attacker without a weapon; the word means soft skill
a Japanese teaching school or family line with its own name and lessons

lessons.title: When the Samurai Class Ended
lessons.mainIdea: After 1868, Japan's new government ended the samurai class, and many jujutsu schools lost students.
reading: In 1868 a new government took power in Japan. This change is called the *Meiji Restoration*. The new leaders wanted railways, factories, an army like Europe's and public schools for all children.
The new government ended the old ranks of society. The samurai, a warrior class, lost their special place. In 1876 a law banned most people from wearing swords in public.
Many old arts looked out of date in this fast new Japan. Some jujutsu teachers lost their students and their pay. Some performed for money. Some ryū closed, and their lessons were nearly lost.

words.d: the 1868 change of government that began fast modern change in Japan
the warrior class of old Japan, ended as a special class after 1868

lessons.title: A Young Student Looks for Teachers
lessons.mainIdea: Kanō Jigorō, born in 1860, studied jujutsu with teachers from two old schools.
reading: *Kanō Jigorō* was born in 1860 in Mikage, near Kobe, Japan. His family moved to Tokyo when he was a boy. He was a strong student in English and other school subjects.
As a teenager, Kanō wanted to study jujutsu. He found a teacher named Fukuda Hachinosuke of the Tenshin Shin'yō-ryū. After Fukuda died, he trained with Iso Masatomo of the same school.
Later Kanō trained with Iikubo Tsunetoshi of the *Kitō-ryū*. Now he knew the lessons of two different schools. He began to compare them and keep what he thought worked best for students.

words.d: the Japanese teacher (1860–1938) who founded judo and the Kodokan
an old jujutsu school that Kanō studied before he made judo

lessons.title: Eishōji Temple, 1882
lessons.mainIdea: In 1882 Kanō opened the Kodokan at a Tokyo temple and named his subject judo.
reading: In 1882 Kanō opened a training room at *Eishōji*, a Buddhist temple in Tokyo. It had only a few mats. He called his school the *Kodokan*. The name means a place for teaching the way.
Kanō named his subject judo, the gentle way. The word ju is the same one in jujutsu. Do means a way or path. Kanō chose do to show that judo was a way of living and learning, not only fighting.
The school moved several times as it grew. It needed bigger rooms for more students. Today the Kodokan Judo Institute stands in the Bunkyō area of Tokyo, and it still keeps judo's official ranks.

words.d: the judo school Kanō founded in Tokyo in 1882; the name means a place for teaching the way
the gentle way; the school sport and subject Kanō made from older jujutsu
the Buddhist temple in Tokyo where the Kodokan first met

lessons.title: Judo as Education
lessons.mainIdea: Kanō said judo should train the body, the mind and good character, like a school subject.
reading: Kanō was a teacher first. In 1889 he gave a talk in Tokyo on judo and education. He said judo could train three things: the body, skill in contests, and the mind and character.

In 1922 Kanō began the Kodokan Culture Society. He used two short phrases to sum up judo. *Seiryoku zen'yō* means best use of energy. *Jita kyōei* means mutual welfare and benefit, or you and others doing well together.
These ideas made judo sound like a school subject. Parents and schools could see a goal beyond winning. Kanō wanted students to use judo lessons in study, work and daily life.

words.d: Kanō's phrase meaning best use of energy
Kanō's phrase meaning mutual welfare and benefit: self and others doing well together

look.title: Kanō on Three Goals
look.text: Judo trains three things. It builds a healthy body. It teaches skill for contests. And it trains the mind and good conduct, so a student can use its lessons in all of life.
look.cite: Kanō Jigorō, lecture on judo and its value in education, Tokyo, 1889

lessons.title: Ranks Anyone Can Read
lessons.mainIdea: The Kodokan used numbered kyū and dan ranks, and the black belt became the sign of dan rank.
reading: Old ryū often marked progress with private scrolls. Kanō used numbered ranks instead. Beginners held *kyū* grades. Advanced students held *dan* grades, counted first dan, second dan and up.
In 1883 Kanō gave the first dan grades. Two of the first were his students Saigō Shirō and Tomita Tsunejirō. Over time, a black belt became the visible sign that a student held a dan rank.
A number is easy to read. A student from one judo club could tell another club what rank they held. The Kodokan kept records of each promotion. This made ranks public, not secret.

words.d: a beginner's grade in judo and many other Japanese arts
an advanced, numbered grade; in judo it is shown with a black belt

look.title: Scroll or Number?
look.text: Old way: a private scroll, tied in a box, read by one teacher's students. Kodokan way: a written rank, like first dan, entered in a record book, shown by a black belt anyone can see.
look.prompt: Which way would help a student who moves to a new city? Explain.

check.why: Kodokan ranks were numbered and kept in records.

lessons.title: Teaching the Teachers
lessons.mainIdea: Kanō led a school that trained teachers, which helped carry judo into Japan's schools.
reading: Kanō worked in education for most of his life. For many years he was the head of the Tokyo Higher Normal School. A *normal school* is a college that trains new teachers.

Teachers trained there went on to schools across Japan. In the early 1900s, Japanese middle schools began to offer judo and kendo, the sword art, as school subjects. Judo now had a place in the school timetable.

Kanō also looked beyond Japan. In 1909 he became the first member from Asia on the International Olympic Committee, called the IOC. He traveled to Europe and the United States many times to speak about judo.

words.d: a college that trains new teachers
the International Olympic Committee, the group that runs the Olympic Games

lessons.title: A World Judo Body
lessons.mainIdea: In 1951 national judo groups formed the International Judo Federation to share one set of rules.
reading: Kanō died in 1938, on a ship coming home from an IOC meeting in Cairo, Egypt. By then judo clubs met in Britain, France and elsewhere in Europe, the Americas and other parts of Asia.

After World War II, national judo groups wanted to hold contests together. In 1951 they formed the *International Judo Federation*, or IJF. A *federation* is a group of member groups that agree on shared rules.
The IJF set rules for world contests. It ran the first World Judo Championships in Tokyo in 1956. The Kodokan still kept ranks in Japan, while the IJF ran world events.

words.d: a group made of member groups, such as national clubs, that agree on shared rules
the world governing body of judo, formed in 1951, also called the IJF

lessons.title: Tokyo 1964
lessons.mainIdea: Judo first became an Olympic sport at the 1964 Tokyo Games, where Anton Geesink won the open class.
reading: Tokyo hosted the Summer Olympics in 1964. Judo was on the program for the first time. The contests were held in the *Nippon Budokan*, a new hall built in Tokyo for martial arts.

There were four events, all for men. Three had *weight classes*, groups of athletes of similar body weight. The fourth was an open class for any weight. Japanese athletes won the three weight-class gold medals.
The open class ended in a surprise. Anton Geesink of the Netherlands beat Kaminaga Akio of Japan for the gold. His win showed that judo now belonged to athletes from many countries.

words.d: the hall in Tokyo built for martial arts, first used for Olympic judo in 1964
a group of athletes of similar body weight who compete against each other

lessons.title: More People on the Mat
lessons.mainIdea: Over the 1900s, more groups gained a place in judo, from a Kodokan women's section to Paralympic judo.
reading: Kanō taught some women judo privately in the early 1900s. In 1926 the Kodokan opened a women's section. Women trained there, but for decades they had few official contests.

*Keiko Fukuda* trained at that women's section in the 1930s. She was the granddaughter of Fukuda Hachinosuke, Kanō's first teacher. She later taught judo in California for many years, and USA Judo named her tenth dan in 2011.
Judo joined the *Paralympic Games* in Seoul in 1988. Paralympic judo is for athletes who are blind or have low vision. Women's judo became an Olympic medal sport in 1992 in Barcelona.

words.d: the world games for athletes with disabilities, held after the Olympics
